evaluation.positioning_hook: After a public panic attack on the House floor, a rising progressive congresswoman cuts a deal with a disgraced lobbyist to save her career—and risks becoming exactly what she campaigned against.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediately legible to adult audiences who follow politics, prestige character drama, and scandal-driven stories. It has a strong topical engine, but the appeal is more adult-skewing than four-quadrant because the pleasure is in insider politics, media spin, and moral compromise.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast: Ada Morris collapses on C-SPAN, the internet turns on her, and she turns to a lobbyist to manage the fallout. The opening bathroom panic attack, the House-floor fainting spell, and the Chris call make the central engine clear within the first act.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ada is a strong lead because she is both aspirational and compromised, and Chris gives the story a slippery counterweight. Quinn, Parker, and Samuel add useful pressure, but the script is still most compelling when Ada is the center of gravity.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script has a fresh angle on political collapse by making the crisis emotional, performative, and media-amplified rather than purely scandal-based. The satire is confident, though the underlying world of D.C. spin and donor politics is familiar terrain.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The first half moves well through the bathroom incident, the office fallout, and the House-floor collapse, but the back half settles into conversation and repositioning more than escalation. The dinner ending is a strong tonal button, yet the feature currently feels more like a setup than a fully escalating arc.

resonant_originality.reasoning: Ada’s collapse on live television is a clean, memorable premise that feels both specific and broadly understandable. The combination of progressive politics, mental-health optics, and lobbying hypocrisy gives the script a recognizable but still ownable twist.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Hill, the office culture, the lobbying bar, and the media-monitoring machinery all feel lived-in and story-generating. The script understands the social codes of D.C. well enough that even small exchanges—like the staffer hierarchy and the op-ed panic—carry texture.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The voice sits in a sharp satirical register with a steady undercurrent of anxiety and humiliation. The contrast between public polish and private breakdown is consistent, and the script knows how to land a cruel joke without losing sympathy for Ada.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material around identity, compromise, and the cost of being a symbolic leader, especially in Ada’s relationship to her base and to tribal politics. At the moment, though, the script mostly surfaces those tensions rather than building a deeper second layer around them.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ada/Quinn and Ada/Parker are functional pressure points, and Chris gives the second half a useful transactional dynamic. Still, the supporting cast is more reactive than generative, so the ensemble energy is solid rather than especially rich.

lead_characters.name: Ada Morris
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, early 30s, progressive congresswoman; ethnically ambiguous / part Native American as referenced in dialogue.
lead_characters.hook: Ada is a rising political star who has learned to perform composure so well that even her breakdowns become part of the image machine. She is charismatic, image-conscious, and genuinely idealistic, but the script keeps exposing the gap between the movement she sold and the compromises she now makes to stay relevant.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Amy Adams in Sharp Objects or Viola Davis in How to Get Away with Murder: a woman whose public control and private fracture are both playable in the same role. It gives an actor the chance to pivot from polished authority to raw panic to moral ambiguity without ever leaving the center of the frame.

lead_characters.name: Quinn Anderson
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, early 20s, young congressional staffer; Dartmouth-educated, left-coded presentation.
lead_characters.hook: Quinn is the bright, earnest junior staffer who still believes political language can mean something clean. She admires Ada, but she also sees the rot underneath the brand, which makes her both loyal and quietly destabilizing.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Auli'i Cravalho in The Power or Haley Lu Richardson in The White Lotus a chance to play intelligence, idealism, and social discomfort at once. The appeal is the close-up work of watching a young staffer realize the system she joined is already asking her to compromise.

lead_characters.name: Parker
lead_characters.demographics: Man, late 40s to early 50s, chief of staff / veteran Hill operator.
lead_characters.hook: Parker is the exhausted professional who has spent so long managing crises that he has turned emotional triage into a personality. He is loyal to Ada in a practical sense, but his real allegiance is to keeping the machine running, even when the machine is embarrassing.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor territory in the vein of Bradley Whitford in The West Wing or Matthew Macfadyen in Succession: dry, controlled, and constantly one beat away from contempt. The role gives an actor the pleasure of playing institutional competence as a form of moral compromise.

lead_characters.name: Samuel
lead_characters.demographics: Man, late 20s, staffer on Ada's team.
lead_characters.hook: Samuel is the anxious, over-caffeinated political aide who speaks in polished damage-control language even when the situation is clearly spiraling. He is useful, nervous, and slightly comic, which makes him a good pressure-release valve inside the office ecosystem.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that lets an actor do fast, precise ensemble work in the mode of Zach Woods in Silicon Valley or Ben Schwartz in The Afterparty. The showcase is timing: selling panic, competence, and self-protective spin in the same breath.

lead_characters.name: Chris Marsh
lead_characters.hook: Chris is a smiling predator in a suit, fluent in bipartisan language and completely at home in transactional corruption. He is funny, sleazy, and self-aware enough to know exactly what he is, which makes him more dangerous rather than less.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the same kind of delicious moral slipperiness as Jeremy Strong in The Big Short or Matthew Macfadyen in Succession, but with more overt charm. The showcase is playing charm as a weapon and letting the audience enjoy the danger.

lead_characters.name: Andy
lead_characters.hook: Andy is Chris’s drinking partner and ideological echo chamber, a man who wraps cynicism in faux-common-sense nostalgia. He helps give the lobbying world a social texture and a second voice of corruption without making the bar scenes feel one-note.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact, scene-stealing supporting part in the vein of Michael Stuhlbarg in The Post or Peter Sarsgaard in The Looming Tower. The appeal is the chance to make a few scenes feel lived-in, funny, and morally gross all at once.

lead_characters.name: Jane
lead_characters.hook: Jane is the young staffer who still believes headlines and hashtags are the same thing as truth. She’s eager, impressionable, and slightly naive, which makes her a useful mirror for the political machine’s self-mythology.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a young actor play ambition before cynicism fully hardens, similar to the early-career energy of Sydney Sweeney in The White Lotus or Kaitlyn Dever in Dopesick. The showcase is the tension between earnestness and the dawning realization that the room is lying to her.

lead_characters.name: Sage
lead_characters.demographics: Teen girl, Native American / tribal youth visitor.
lead_characters.hook: Sage is the starstruck constituent who briefly embodies the idealized version of Ada’s political promise. Her admiration is sincere, which makes the later political disillusionment around Ada sting more sharply.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small but emotionally legible part that gives a young actor a clean, memorable beat of awe and vulnerability, in the mode of the best one-scene turns in prestige drama. The showcase is sincerity: making the audience feel what Ada used to mean.

lead_characters.name: Rep. Jones
lead_characters.hook: Rep. Jones is the cold, dismissive institutional antagonist who barely needs dialogue to communicate the old guard’s contempt. He functions as a quick, efficient symbol of the hostility Ada faces across the aisle.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sharp, low-page-count role for a seasoned actor who can project status and disdain instantly, like the best recurring political antagonists in The West Wing or Veep. The appeal is economy: a few beats that define a whole worldview.

lead_characters.name: Rep. Goldman
lead_characters.hook: Rep. Goldman is the procedural authority who tries to restore order when Ada collapses on the floor. He is less a character study than a pressure point in the machinery of public crisis.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play institutional command under live-fire pressure, similar to the emergency-room authority figures in prestige ensemble pieces. The showcase is controlled urgency.

casting_characteristics: lead requires a woman in her early 30s who can play polished public charisma and private panic
Ada is described as ethnically ambiguous / part Native American in dialogue
supporting cast skews toward late-20s to late-60s political professionals

technical.vfx_details: No visible VFX requirements beyond standard cleanup and broadcast-screen inserts.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical medical handling for the collapse, wheelchair movement, and crowd reaction on the House floor.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; contemporary political character drama with a contained production footprint.

budget.note: Contemporary interiors, a small number of Washington locations, no VFX-heavy sequences, and no action set pieces keep this comfortably contained.

casting.note: The lead role needs an actor who can sell elite political polish, public likability, and a credible panic attack without losing authority. Chris also benefits from a very specific kind of charming sleaze.

development.note: The central engine is clear, but the feature currently plays like a strong first-half escalation into a quieter transactional ending. Buyers will look for a more forceful final movement around Ada's moral turn and what it costs her.

comp_set.title: Vice
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the political satire lane, the appetite for institutional cynicism, and the pleasure of watching power operate as performance.

comp_set.title: The Assistant
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the contained, pressure-cooker workplace texture and the way small procedural spaces reveal larger systems of power.

comp_set.title: The Post
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on newsroom-adjacent public-image politics, institutional stakes, and a prestige adult audience that likes policy as drama.

comp_set.title: Bombshell
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the media-fallout structure and the way public scandal becomes a character-driven crisis with broad adult appeal.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like prestige political dramas, media scandal stories, and sharp workplace satire with a female lead at the center.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 30-60, educated, urban/suburban, with a slight female lean and strong appeal to viewers who follow politics and current affairs.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary Washington interiors, a modest cast, and no meaningful VFX keep this in the specialty indie range.

types_of_buyers: specialty distributors looking for adult awards-leaning material
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally beside adult political satire and workplace-pressure dramas that sell on performance, topicality, and a clean high-concept premise. The script is especially attractive to buyers who want a contained, actor-forward feature with a timely public-image hook.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; no clear sequel, prequel, or spinoff vector beyond the central Ada/Chris story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ada's collapse is a clean, cinematic hook.
strengths.what_it_means: The script has an instantly marketable inciting image that can sell the movie in a single sentence and a single trailer beat. That makes it attractive to buyers looking for a topical prestige feature with a memorable public breakdown as the engine.
strengths.evidence: The bathroom panic attack, the House-floor fainting spell, and the C-SPAN fallout all arrive early and define the premise.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The lead role is a showcase for contradiction.
strengths.what_it_means: Ada is built to attract an actor who wants prestige material with range: public charisma, private fragility, political calculation, and moral self-recognition. That kind of role can anchor financing and give the project a clear packaging path.
strengths.evidence: Ada reassures constituents, manages staff, collapses in private, then admits she misses being a radical and knows she is selling out.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The D.C. world feels specific and usable.
strengths.what_it_means: The office hierarchy, media panic, Hill etiquette, and lobbying ecosystem create a setting that can generate scenes without expensive scope. Buyers get a contained world with enough texture to feel premium rather than generic.
strengths.evidence: The staff room, the lobbying bar, the House floor, and the hospital-room damage control all feel like distinct nodes in one political machine.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Chris gives the second half a sharp transactional engine.
strengths.what_it_means: Once Chris enters as a fixer-lobbyist, the movie gains a morally slippery counterpart who can drive scenes through negotiation rather than exposition. That broadens the packaging appeal because the film is no longer only about collapse; it becomes about who profits from it.
strengths.evidence: Chris calls Ada after the scandal, offers help, and turns the crisis into leverage around the vote and the hazardous-waste site.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The satire lands without losing sympathy.
strengths.what_it_means: The script can play the absurdity of political language, media spin, and bipartisan corruption while still keeping Ada emotionally legible. That balance is valuable in the marketplace because it widens the audience beyond pure political insiders.
strengths.evidence: The dialogue around asthma versus mental breakdown, the staffer spin, and the lobbying-bar banter all keep the tone biting but not alienating.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, actor-forward political satire with a built-in trailer image: a rising congresswoman collapses on live TV and has to buy her way back into power. The combination of a showcase lead role, contemporary Washington texture, and a modest production footprint makes it a credible prestige-indie package with streamer appeal.

items.area: The back half softens after the collapse.
items.detail: The House-floor fainting spell is a strong midpoint-style event, but the script then spends a lot of time in damage control, phone calls, and dinner conversation. For a feature, that creates a buying conversation around whether the second half has enough escalation to match the opening engine.

items.area: Ada's final turn is more transactional than dramatic.
items.detail: The Chris dinner lands as intimate and unsettling, but it reads more like a mood shift than a decisive climax. Buyers will notice that the movie ends on a compromise rather than a fully sharpened consequence for Ada's public collapse and political identity.

items.area: Quinn and Parker are functional, not yet indispensable.
items.detail: Both characters help externalize the office pressure, but neither yet has enough independent momentum to create a stronger ensemble engine around Ada. That keeps the film firmly lead-driven, which is fine, but it limits the relational richness the package can advertise.

items.area: The political stakes stay somewhat abstract.
items.detail: The op-ed backlash, the labor vote, and the hazardous-waste site are all credible pressure points, but they remain more symbolic than visceral on the page. A producer will weigh whether the audience feels the cost of Ada's compromise beyond the reputational damage.

issues.headline: The script has a strong premise and a very castable lead, but the feature currently peaks early and then settles into damage-control scenes that feel smaller than the opening promise. The main greenlight question is whether the Ada/Chris dynamic can carry a more forceful second-half turn than the page currently delivers.
